intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene (607429) on chromosome 10p12.

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: PDSS1 defect has been described in three patients from two families 6, 7 carrying three pathogenic variants in the PDSS1 gene, homozygous in one family and compound heterozygote in the other (Table 1).
checks.explanation: The paper describes homozygous and compound heterozygous PDSS1 variants that cause CoQ10 deficiency. The COQ10D2 label is standard nomenclature.

checks.claim: The PDSS1 gene is located on chromosome 10p12.
checks.evidence_quote: PDSS1 and PDSS2 genes encode two proteins (DPS1 and DLP1) implied in the first step of CoQ10 synthesis
checks.explanation: The paper does not give a location, but the instructions treat a gene's chromosomal location as standard nomenclature, which counts as supported.

paragraphs.text: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is an autosomal recessive disorder of CoQ10 biosynthesis. The phenotype varies. Some patients have sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy, with mild intellectual disability, muscle weakness, and valvulopathy. Others have a severe, progressive multisystem disorder that can include leukoencephalopathy, nephrotic syndrome, and death in early childhood (Nardecchia et al., 2021; Bellusci et al., 2021).

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is an autosomal recessive disorder of CoQ10 biosynthesis.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations in the genes encoding for these enzymes cause a CoQ10 deficiency, characterized by neurological and systemic symptoms.
checks.explanation: The paper describes a disorder of CoQ10 biosynthesis with homozygous and compound heterozygous variants, but it never explicitly calls the inheritance autosomal recessive.

checks.claim: The COQ10D2 phenotype is variable.
checks.evidence_quote: PDSS1 deficiency is a clinically heterogenous rare disorder
checks.explanation: The paper calls the disorder clinically heterogeneous.

checks.claim: Some patients with COQ10D2 have sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy, with mild intellectual disability, muscle weakness, and valvulopathy.

checks.explanation: This matches the Mollet sibs as the paper describes them.

checks.explanation: The paper describes a severe phenotype with leukoencephalopathy, nephrotic syndrome and early death, but it does not use the words 'progressive multisystem'.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) reported 2 sisters born to consanguineous Egyptian parents. The proband was 16 years old. Her motor development was normal, but her language was severely delayed, and profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss was found at age 4 years. She later had mild intellectual disability. Her vision then declined progressively: visual acuity was normal at age 11 years and 1/10 bilaterally at age 14 years. She also had red-green dyschromatopsia, optic atrophy mainly in the inferior temporal sector, abnormal VEPs, and reduced retinal nerve fiber layer thickness on OCT. Other findings were diffuse mild muscle weakness, mild postural tremor of the upper limbs, and a moderately dysplastic mitral valve with moderate insufficiency and tricuspid insufficiency. Brain MRI was normal. Her younger sister, age 6 years, had bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. At age 6 years she also developed decreased visual acuity, and examination showed optic atrophy with bilateral temporal pallor of the optic nerve head and divergent strabismus. In both sisters, as in the sibs reported by Mollet et al. (2007), the hearing loss came before the optic atrophy.

paragraphs.text: Bellusci et al. (2021) described a boy with primary CoQ10 deficiency. He was born prematurely after in vitro fertilization, and the pregnancy was complicated by twin-twin transfusion. At 5 months of age he had failure to thrive, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, bilateral hearing impairment, pulmonary hypertension, livedo reticularis, and chronic distal phalangeal erythema. He went on to develop a progressive multisystem disorder with severe developmental delay, pyramidal dysfunction, seizures, tremor, optic atrophy, nystagmus, severe visual and hearing impairment, cystic white matter changes, and chronic heart failure. He died at 3 years of age. Brain MRI showed mild cerebral atrophy at 12 months. At 24 months it showed cystic change in the white matter, with signal abnormalities and small necrotic or porencephalic cysts in the white matter tracts surrounding the lateral ventricles and commissural fibers; the U fibers, pyramidal tracts, and gray matter were spared.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) used whole-exome sequencing in 2 Egyptian sisters with sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy. They identified a homozygous c.735G-T transversion in the PDSS1 gene, resulting in a gln245-to-his (Q245H) substitution. The variant affects a highly conserved residue, was absent from gnomAD, and lay within a 12-Mb region of homozygosity. Both parents carried the variant. Of the unaffected sibs, one sister was homozygous wildtype and one brother was heterozygous. Sanger sequencing of the OPA1, OPA3, and WFS1 genes found no pathogenic variants.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) compared their patients with the 3 previously reported patients with PDSS1 deficiency from 2 families. Their homozygous Q245H patients resembled the 2 sibs homozygous for D308E reported by Mollet et al. (2007): all had deafness, optic atrophy, mild intellectual disability, and muscle weakness, with hearing loss coming before optic atrophy. In contrast, the patient reported by Vasta et al. (2012), who was compound heterozygous for a missense and a truncating variant, had a much more severe phenotype, with leukoencephalopathy and nephrotic syndrome, and died at age 16 months.

checks.claim: Nardecchia et al. (2021) compared their PDSS1-deficient patients with the 3 previously reported patients with PDSS1 deficiency from 2 families.
checks.evidence_quote: PDSS1 defect has been described in three patients from two families 6, 7 carrying three pathogenic variants in the PDSS1 gene, homozygous in one family and compound heterozygote in the other (Table 1).
checks.explanation: The Discussion and Table 1 compare the present cases with the 3 earlier patients from 2 families.

checks.claim: Patients homozygous for the PDSS1 Q245H variant reported by Nardecchia et al. (2021) resembled the 2 sibs homozygous for the PDSS1 D308E variant.

checks.evidence_quote: Sequencing of PDSS1 identified a homozygous nucleotide substitution modifying a conserved amino acid of the protein (D308E).

checks.evidence_quote: Optic atrophy | + | + | ND | + | +
checks.explanation: Table 1 marks optic atrophy as present in all four homozygous patients.

checks.evidence_quote: Developmental impairment | Mild intellectual disability | Mild intellectual disability | Developmental delay | Mild intellectual disability | Mild intellectual disability
checks.explanation: Table 1 lists mild intellectual disability for all four homozygous patients.

paragraphs.text: Bellusci et al. (2021) noted that their PDSS1 patient had phalangeal erythema, livedo reticularis, and pulmonary hypertension together. They suggested that this combination pointed to microvascular dysfunction as a possible underlying mechanism.

checks.evidence_quote: The coexistence in our case of phalangeal erythema, livedo reticularis, and pulmonary hypertension suggests microvascular dysfunction as a possible underlying physiopathogenic mechanism.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) proposed that PDSS1 deficiency, which is clinically heterogeneous, be added to the differential diagnosis of optic atrophy with sensorineural deafness. They noted that in PDSS1 deficiency the deafness appears to begin before the optic atrophy, unlike in OPA1 and OPA3 defects. They also stated that CoQ10 synthesis defects should be considered treatable conditions.

checks.explanation: The paper calls PDSS1 deficiency clinically heterogeneous.

checks.claim: In PDSS1 deficiency, deafness appears to begin before optic atrophy, unlike in OPA1 and OPA3 defects.
checks.evidence_quote: In contrast to OPA1 and OPA3 defects, the onset of sensorineural deafness seems to precede the optic atrophy in PDSS1, hallmarking this particular form.
checks.explanation: The paper contrasts PDSS1 with OPA1 and OPA3 defects in this way.

paragraphs.text: Bellusci et al. (2021) treated their patient with oral ubidecarenone (CoQ10) at 15 mg/kg/day from 5 months of age and increased the dose to 30 mg/kg/day after the molecular diagnosis. The high-dose supplementation did not control disease progression, and the patient died at 3 years of age.

Yeast Deltacoq1 strains transformed with mutant yeast COQ1 grew poorly on respiratory medium.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sisters born to consanguineous Egyptian parents, who had sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy, Nardecchia et al. (2021) identified a homozygous c.735G-T transversion in the PDSS1 gene, resulting in a gln245-to-his (Q245H) substitution at a highly conserved residue. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and was absent from gnomAD. Both parents were heterozygous, an unaffected sister was homozygous wildtype, and an unaffected brother was heterozygous.

checks.claim: Nardecchia et al. (2021) reported 2 sisters born to consanguineous Egyptian parents with sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we describe two young sisters with sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy, due to a novel homozygous pathogenic variant in PDSS1.
checks.explanation: The case description adds that the parents were consanguineous and Egyptian.

checks.claim: The 2 Egyptian sisters carried a homozygous c.735G-T transversion in PDSS1, resulting in a gln245-to-his (Q245H) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: A whole‐exome sequencing analysis revealed a homozygous likely pathogenic missense variant c.735G > T in the PDSS1 gene, never reported in the public database GnomAD. This variant causes the amino acid change p.Gln245His
checks.explanation: The variant and protein change match.

checks.claim: PDSS1 Q245H affects a highly conserved residue.
checks.evidence_quote: in a highly conserved position (98.5%, Fig. 1A).
checks.explanation: The residue is highly conserved.

checks.explanation: The variant was found by whole-exome sequencing.

checks.explanation: Segregation was confirmed in both parents. With homozygous affected children and unaffected parents, the parents must be heterozygous.
